column1: Why does the Companies Act define a "small company" by paid-up capital AND turnover thresholds?
column2: To ring-fence genuinely small firms for lighter compliance; both tests must be met so a low-capital but high-turnover firm can't escape scrutiny. Limits: capital up to Rs.4 crore, turnover up to Rs.40 crore.

column1: What are the paid-up capital and turnover limits for a "small company" (Sec 2(85))?
column2: Paid-up capital not exceeding Rs.4 crore and turnover not exceeding Rs.40 crore (as per latest rules).

column1: Why can a public company never be a "small company"?
column2: Small-company relief is meant for closely-held private firms; public companies invite public investment, so they always need full compliance regardless of size.

column1: What is the minimum number of members for a private vs public company?
column2: Private: minimum 2; Public: minimum 7. (OPC needs just 1.)

column1: What is the maximum number of members in a private company, and why?
column2: 200 (excluding employees/ex-employees who are members). The cap keeps it closely-held, distinguishing it from a public company that raises capital widely.

column1: Why is a One Person Company (OPC) restricted to a natural person who is an Indian resident?
column2: To keep the single-owner structure genuinely individual and locally accountable; a body corporate can't hide behind an OPC. Resident = stay of 120 days or more in previous FY.

column1: What triggers mandatory conversion of an OPC into a private/public company?
column2: Earlier the paid-up capital/turnover ceilings applied, but those thresholds were removed; OPC may convert voluntarily anytime, and must if it wants to raise public capital.

column1: Why does Sec 2(87) treat control of the Board's composition as "control" for a subsidiary?
column2: Because economic ownership isn't the only power; whoever appoints/removes a majority of directors effectively runs the company, so that alone makes it a subsidiary.

column1: When is a company a "subsidiary" under Sec 2(87)?
column2: If the holding company controls Board composition OR holds/controls more than one-half of the total voting power.

column1: Why can a subsidiary not hold shares in its holding company (Sec 19)?
column2: To prevent circular shareholding that would let a company indirectly buy its own shares and inflate its capital artificially.

column1: What is the doctrine of "lifting the corporate veil"?
column2: Courts disregard separate legal personality when the company form is used for fraud, tax evasion, or to defeat law, holding the real persons behind it liable.

column1: Why is a company said to have "perpetual succession"?
column2: Its existence is independent of members; death, insolvency or exit of members doesn't end it. Only law can dissolve it. Members may come and go; the company continues.

column1: Why must a company incorporated for charitable purposes under Sec 8 not pay dividends?
column2: Its licence requires profits be applied only to promote its objects; distributing profit would defeat the not-for-profit purpose that earned it exemptions.

column1: What is the "doctrine of ultra vires"?
column2: Acts beyond the objects clause of the memorandum are void and cannot be ratified even by all shareholders, protecting creditors and investors from mission drift.

column1: Why is the memorandum called the "charter" of a company?
column2: It defines the company's constitution, powers, and scope of activities toward outsiders; it's the foundational document limiting what the company can do.

column1: What is the "doctrine of constructive notice"?
column2: Outsiders dealing with a company are deemed to know its public documents (MOA/AOA); they can't claim ignorance of registered limits on the company's powers.

column1: What is the "doctrine of indoor management" (Turquand rule)?
column2: Outsiders may assume internal procedures were properly followed; they aren't bound to verify internal compliance, protecting them where directors flout internal rules.

column1: What is the reserved-word rule for a company using "One Person Company"?
column2: The words "(One Person Company)" must appear in brackets below the company's name wherever printed/engraved.

column1: Why does Sec 12 require the registered office within 30 days of incorporation?
column2: The company must have a fixed address to receive legal communications from day one; it's the point of official service and record inspection.

column1: What is the time limit to file a change of registered office within the same state but different ROC jurisdiction?
column2: Requires Regional Director approval; confirmation to be filed and registered within the prescribed period, then intimated to ROC.

column1: Why must every prospectus state facts fully and truly (Sec 26)?
column2: Investors rely on it to decide; concealment or misstatement invites civil and criminal liability because capital is being raised from the public on that trust.

column1: What is a "deemed prospectus" (Sec 25)?
column2: When a company allots securities to an issuing house intending they be offered to the public, the offer document is treated as a prospectus issued by the company.

column1: What is the "golden legal rule" for prospectus disclosure?
column2: Those issuing a prospectus stand in a fiduciary position and must disclose the whole truth with strictest accuracy; nothing should be stated as fact that isn't.

column1: Why is a "shelf prospectus" allowed for certain issuers?
column2: To let frequent issuers (e.g., banks, NBFCs) raise capital in tranches without a fresh prospectus each time; valid up to one year, updated via an information memorandum.

column1: What is minimum subscription and why is 90% the benchmark?
column2: The minimum amount stated in the prospectus that must be subscribed before allotment; 90% of the issue must be received, else money is refunded, ensuring viability.

column1: Why must application money be at least 5% of nominal value of the security?
column2: SEBI/Act require a minimum stake at application to filter non-serious applicants and ensure genuine commitment before allotment.

column1: What is the time limit to refund application money if minimum subscription is not received?
column2: Within 15 days from closure of the issue; beyond that, interest at 15% p.a. is payable.

column1: Why does Sec 42 restrict a private placement to 200 persons in a financial year?
column2: Beyond 200 it becomes a de facto public offer; the cap prevents companies from circumventing prospectus and public-issue safeguards.

column1: What identifiable persons are excluded from the 200-person private placement cap?
column2: Qualified Institutional Buyers (QIBs) and employees under ESOP are excluded from the count.

column1: Why must private placement money go into a separate bank account and not be utilised before allotment?
column2: To protect subscribers' funds and ensure money is used only for the stated purpose after valid allotment; premature use is a serious contravention.

column1: What is the time limit to allot securities under private placement and file return of allotment?
column2: Allot within 60 days of receiving application money; file PAS-3 within 15 days of allotment.

column1: Why can't a company issue shares at a discount (Sec 53)?
column2: It would defraud creditors by understating the capital cushion; issue at discount is void, except sweat equity shares which are a permitted exception.

column1: What are "sweat equity shares" and why permitted at discount?
column2: Shares issued to directors/employees for know-how or value additions; permitted because they reward genuine contribution rather than dilute creditor protection.

column1: Why is the securities premium a capital reserve with restricted uses (Sec 52)?
column2: It represents shareholders' capital contribution above par, not distributable profit; usable only for specified purposes like issuing bonus shares or writing off issue expenses.

column1: List permitted uses of the Securities Premium Account.
column2: Issue fully paid bonus shares; write off preliminary expenses; write off issue expenses/commission/discount on debentures; premium on redemption of preference shares/debentures; buy-back.

column1: Why does Sec 62 mandate a rights issue before fresh equity to existing shareholders?
column2: To protect existing shareholders' proportionate ownership and voting rights from dilution; they get first right to maintain their stake.

column1: What is the notice period and minimum offer window for a rights issue under Sec 62?
column2: Offer by notice specifying shares and a period of not less than 15 days and not more than 30 days to accept.

column1: Why must a company create a Capital Redemption Reserve when redeeming preference shares out of profits (Sec 55)?
column2: To replace the capital being paid out, keeping the creditors' buffer intact; CRR equals the nominal value redeemed and is treated like paid-up capital.

column1: Why can preference shares be redeemed only if fully paid?
column2: Partly-paid shares carry uncalled liability; redeeming them would extinguish that safeguard for creditors before the money is even collected.

column1: What is the maximum tenure for redeemable preference shares?
column2: 20 years generally; up to 30 years for infrastructure projects (redeeming at least 10% per year from the 21st year).

column1: Why does buy-back require the debt-equity ratio to stay within 2:1 after buy-back (Sec 68)?
column2: To ensure the company doesn't erode its capital base and over-leverage, protecting creditors when it returns cash to shareholders.

column1: What are the key buy-back limits under Sec 68?
column2: Up to 25% of paid-up capital and free reserves (10% if Board-only approval); 25% of paid-up equity in a year; debt-equity max 2:1; funded from free reserves/securities premium/proceeds of fresh issue.

column1: Why is there a 1-year cooling-off before a company can make another buy-back?
column2: To prevent repeated capital erosion and market manipulation; ensures buy-back is a considered capital decision, not a routine share-price prop.

column1: Why must a company transfer to Capital Redemption Reserve on buy-back out of free reserves?
column2: Same logic as preference redemption: capital paid out is replaced by CRR so the creditor cushion is preserved.

column1: Why does Sec 71 require creating a Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR)?
column2: Debentures are borrowings that must be repaid; DRR earmarks profits so redemption isn't funded by fresh borrowing, protecting debenture-holders.

column1: What distinguishes a debenture from a share?
column2: A debenture is a creditor's instrument (fixed interest, repayable, no ownership/voting) whereas a share is ownership (dividend, voting, residual claim, generally non-repayable).

column1: Why does Sec 73 broadly prohibit companies from accepting deposits from the public?
column2: Past scams showed public deposits are risky without banking-style safeguards; only eligible public companies with strict conditions may accept them.

column1: What conditions let a private company accept deposits from members (Sec 73)?
column2: Pass resolution, issue circular, file with ROC, provide deposit insurance/security, maintain deposit repayment reserve of 20% of deposits maturing next FY in a separate bank account.

column1: What is the Deposit Repayment Reserve Account requirement?
column2: On or before 30th April each year, deposit at least 20% of deposits maturing during the following financial year in a scheduled bank; usable only for repayment.

column1: Why are certain receipts (e.g., advance for goods, share application money) excluded from "deposit"?
column2: They're genuine commercial transactions, not borrowings; treating them as deposits would choke normal business and misapply investor-protection rules.

column1: Why must charges be registered within 30 days of creation (Sec 77)?
column2: Registration gives public notice to creditors of prior claims on assets; unregistered charges are void against the liquidator and other creditors.

column1: What is the extended time to register a charge beyond the initial 30 days?
column2: Registrar may allow registration within 60 days on payment of additional fees, and a further 60 days (total 120) with ad valorem fees, on application.

column1: What is the consequence of a charge remaining unregistered?
column2: The charge is void against the liquidator and creditors; the money still remains payable, but the security (priority) is lost.

column1: Why must every company hold its first AGM within 9 months of the first financial year-end?
column2: To give members an early account of the company's affairs; the longer window recognises a new company needs time to close its first, possibly long, accounting period.

column1: What are the AGM timing rules (Sec 96)?
column2: First AGM within 9 months of first FY-end; subsequent AGMs within 6 months of FY-end, max gap 15 months between two AGMs, held in business hours (9am-6pm) on a non-national-holiday.

column1: Why is the quorum for a public company's general meeting tiered by member count (Sec 103)?
column2: Fairness and practicality: larger companies need more members present to be representative, so quorum scales 5/15/30 for up to 1000/5000/over 5000 members.

column1: What is the quorum for a private company general meeting?
column2: 2 members personally present, regardless of total membership.

column1: Why does an ordinary resolution need only a simple majority while special needs 75%?
column2: Routine matters warrant majority rule; fundamental changes (altering MOA/AOA, reducing capital) need a supermajority to protect minority from drastic decisions.

column1: What notice period is required for a general meeting, and can it be shorter?
column2: 21 clear days' notice; shorter notice is valid if consent of 95% of members entitled to vote is obtained.

column1: Why is a proxy allowed to attend but generally not to speak or vote on a show of hands?
column2: A proxy is a stand-in for voting rights, not a member; the law lets absent members exercise their vote without giving proxies full participatory rights.

column1: What is the limit on proxies one person can hold (Sec 105)?
column2: A proxy can act for max 50 members and holding in aggregate not more than 10% of total share capital carrying voting rights.

column1: Why must minutes of meetings be recorded within 30 days (Sec 118)?
column2: Minutes are legal evidence of decisions; timely, accurate recording prevents disputes and manipulation of what the meeting actually resolved.

column1: Why does Sec 123 permit dividend only out of profits (current or accumulated) or money provided by government?
column2: Dividend is a distribution of profit, not capital; paying from capital would defraud creditors by returning their security to shareholders.

column1: What must be done with declared dividend not paid/claimed within 30 days?
column2: Transfer to a special "Unpaid Dividend Account" within 7 days after the 30 days; amounts unclaimed for 7 years go to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF).

column1: Why does dividend declaration require transfer of unclaimed amounts to IEPF after 7 years?
column2: To channel long-abandoned funds to investor protection/education rather than let companies retain them indefinitely; shares too are transferred to IEPF.

column1: Why can't a company declare dividend if it has failed to comply with deposit repayment (Sec 123)?
column2: Creditors/depositors rank ahead of shareholders; a company in default on repayments cannot reward owners before settling its obligations.

column1: Why must financial statements give a "true and fair view" (Sec 129)?
column2: So stakeholders get an honest economic picture; compliance with format alone isn't enough if it misleads, hence substance over mere form.

column1: Why does Sec 135 mandate CSR spending of 2% of average net profits for qualifying companies?
column2: To make profitable large companies contribute to social development; it institutionalises corporate responsibility rather than leaving it voluntary.

column1: What are the CSR applicability thresholds (Sec 135)?
column2: Net worth Rs.500 crore or more, OR turnover Rs.1000 crore or more, OR net profit Rs.5 crore or more, in the immediately preceding financial year.

column1: What happens to unspent CSR amount (other than ongoing projects)?
column2: Transfer to a Schedule VII fund within 6 months of FY-end. For ongoing projects, transfer to a special Unspent CSR Account within 30 days, to be spent within 3 years.

column1: Why does Sec 138 require internal audit for prescribed companies?
column2: Large/complex operations need an independent check on internal controls to catch errors/fraud early, beyond the annual statutory audit.

column1: Why is the auditor appointed for 5 years and rotated (Sec 139)?
column2: A fixed term ensures independence from year-to-year pressure, while mandatory rotation prevents cosy long-term relationships that erode objectivity.

column1: What are the auditor rotation limits for prescribed companies (Sec 139(2))?
column2: Individual auditor: one term of 5 years; audit firm: two terms of 5 years (10 years); then a 5-year cooling-off before reappointment.

column1: Why does Sec 141 disqualify an auditor who holds securities in the company?
column2: Financial interest compromises independence; an auditor with a stake may soften findings that hurt share value, defeating the audit's purpose.

column1: List key auditor disqualifications under Sec 141.
column2: Body corporate (except LLP), officer/employee of company, partner/employee of such, holding security or indebted above Rs.5 lakh, business relationship, convicted of fraud (10-yr bar).

column1: Why does Sec 143 give the auditor a duty to report fraud to the Central Government?
column2: To make the auditor a gatekeeper against fraud; frauds above Rs.1 crore must be reported to CG, ensuring serious misconduct isn't buried in the audit file.

column1: What is the fraud-reporting threshold that goes to the Central Government under Sec 143(12)?
column2: Fraud involving Rs.1 crore or more: report to Central Government; below Rs.1 crore: report to the Board/Audit Committee and disclose in Board's report.

column1: Why must an auditor state whether the company has adequate internal financial controls?
column2: Controls prevent misstatement and fraud; the auditor's opinion on IFC gives stakeholders assurance the numbers rest on a sound control system.

column1: Why is the "General Clauses Act, 1897" called a consolidating and interpretation statute?
column2: It defines common terms and lays down default interpretation rules so every other Act need not repeat them, ensuring consistency across the statute book.

column1: Under the General Clauses Act, how is a period "from" a date computed?
column2: The first day is excluded and the last day included (unless a contrary intention appears), so "within 30 days from X" starts counting the day after X.

column1: Under the General Clauses Act, what if the last day for an act falls on a holiday?
column2: The act is valid if done on the next working day when the office reopens; a closed office can't be held against the person.

column1: What does "shall" vs "may" signify in statutory interpretation?
column2: Shall is generally mandatory (must be obeyed) while "may" is directory/enabling (discretionary), though context and purpose can reverse the presumption.

column1: What is the "literal/grammatical rule" of interpretation?
column2: Words are given their ordinary, natural meaning; if the language is plain, the court applies it even if the result seems harsh, respecting legislative supremacy.

column1: What is the "mischief rule" (Heydon's case)?
column2: The court asks what defect/mischief the law aimed to cure and interprets the statute to suppress that mischief and advance the remedy.

column1: What is the "golden rule" of interpretation?
column2: Start with the literal meaning but depart from it just enough to avoid absurdity, repugnance, or inconsistency the legislature could not have intended.

column1: What is the rule of "ejusdem generis"?
column2: General words following specific ones of a class are limited to that same class; e.g., "cars, trucks and other vehicles" means other motor vehicles, not aircraft.

column1: What is "noscitur a sociis"?
column2: A word's meaning is known from its companions; ambiguous words take colour from surrounding words in the provision.

column1: What is the difference between a "proviso", an "explanation" and an "illustration"?
column2: Proviso carves out an exception to the main clause; explanation clarifies/expands meaning; illustration gives an example aiding understanding (but can't override the section).

column1: Why is the "preamble" a useful aid to interpretation?
column2: It states the object and purpose of the Act; when words are ambiguous, the preamble guides the court toward the intended meaning, though it can't override clear text.

column1: What is the objective of FEMA, 1999 (as opposed to FERA)?
column2: FEMA facilitates external trade/payments and orderly forex market development; it treats violations as civil (compoundable), unlike FERA's criminal, control-oriented regime.

column1: What is the difference between a "capital account transaction" and a "current account transaction" under FEMA?
column2: Capital account transactions alter assets/liabilities outside India (or of non-residents in India); current account transactions are all others, e.g., trade payments, travel, interest.

column1: Why are current account transactions generally free under FEMA while capital ones are regulated?
column2: Current transactions are routine trade/service flows essential to commerce; capital flows can destabilise the economy/exchange rate, so RBI regulates them.

column1: Who is a "person resident in India" under FEMA?
column2: One residing in India for more than 182 days in the preceding financial year (subject to purpose-of-stay exceptions), plus specified offices/agencies/companies in India.

column1: Why does FEMA determine residency by days of stay rather than citizenship?
column2: FEMA regulates economic activity/forex flows tied to where a person actually operates, so physical presence (182+ days) matters more than nationality.

column1: Why is contravention under FEMA "compoundable"?
column2: FEMA aims to manage forex, not punish; letting parties settle contraventions by paying a penalty (compounding) keeps trade flowing and reduces litigation.

column1: Why must a Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) have at least two designated partners, one resident in India?
column2: Designated partners bear compliance responsibility; requiring a resident ensures there's always someone locally accountable to regulators.

column1: Why is an LLP a "body corporate" with perpetual succession unlike an ordinary partnership?
column2: The LLP Act gives it separate legal personality, so partners' liability is limited and the entity survives partner changes, combining company and partnership benefits.

column1: Why is a partner in an LLP generally not liable for another partner's wrongful acts?
column2: Limited liability is the LLP's core benefit; a partner is shielded from others' misconduct done without their knowledge, unlike unlimited joint liability in a firm.

column1: What is the minimum and maximum number of partners in an LLP?
column2: Minimum 2 partners; no maximum limit (unlike a private company's 200-member cap).

column1: Why does the LLP Act still make a partner liable for their own fraud despite limited liability?
column2: Limited liability protects against others' acts, not one's own wrongdoing; allowing escape from personal fraud would make the shield a licence to cheat.
